news.content: August 3, 2026 at 20:21:38 SGGP Online SGGP Thể Thao SGGP Đầu tư Tài chính 中文版 SGGP Epaper SGGP English Edition Trang chủ National Ho Chi Minh City International Business Business Banking-finance Economy Self - introduction Stock market Highlights Vietnam's FDI inflows surge 58 percent to US$38 billion in seven months Agricultural, forestry, fishery exports rise 7.5 percent in first seven months Latest August stocks seen gaining, but caution advised August 3, 2026 at 09:09:00 Ho Chi Minh City launches retail stimulus to boost purchasing power August 3, 2026 at 09:14:04 Government targets MSCI stock market upgrade, fintech sandbox by 2030 August 3, 2026 at 03:37:52 Health Education Sports Culture/art Law Science/technology Lifestyle Travel Weather Health Health Ministry issues urgent advisory as Covid-19, seasonal flu cases surge SGGP July 29, 2026 at 07:09:10 The Ministry of Health issued a press release on July 28 outlining prevention measures against Covid-19 and seasonal influenza, warning of a heightened risk of respiratory disease transmission across the country. Doctors collect samples from Covid-19 patients. (Photo: SGGP) Data from the national infectious disease surveillance system and reports from major hospitals, including the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, indicate a rising trend in Covid-19 consultations and admissions in recent weeks. However, health officials emphasized that there has been no unusual spike in severe cases or fatalities related to the virus. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the NB.1.8.1 variant, an Omicron sub-lineage, remained the dominant circulating strain globally and across the Western Pacific region through late June 2026. Current evidence suggests the variant neither causes more severe illness nor significantly diminishes the effectiveness of existing public health protocols. The spike coincides with Vietnam’s peak summer travel season. Increased domestic mobility, holiday gatherings, and crowded public events, combined with hot, humid weather that drives people indoors into poorly ventilated, air-conditioned spaces, have created fertile ground for the spread of airborne pathogens. Nevertheless, the risk of severe complications remains elevated for vulnerable populations, including the elderly, young children, pregnant women, and individuals with compromised immune systems or underlying conditions such as cardiovascular disease, chronic lung disease, and diabetes. news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical The Ministry of Health advises on preventing COVID-19 and seasonal influenza. VTV.vn - With the number of COVID-19 cases trending upwards in recent weeks, the Ministry of Health advises people to proactively take preventive measures, especially those at high risk. Đài truyền hình Việt Nam•29/07/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Illustration. The Department of Disease Prevention ( Ministry of Health ) reported that the number of COVID-19 cases seeking examination and treatment at several medical facilities has tended to increase in recent weeks. However, to date, no unusual increase in severe cases or deaths has been recorded. You may also like According to the World Health Organization (WHO), by the end of June 2026, the NB.1.8.1 variant – a subtype of Omicron – was circulating primarily globally and in the Western Pacific region. There is currently no evidence to suggest that this variant causes more severe illness or reduces the effectiveness of existing disease control measures. The Ministry of Health notes that the summer vacation period, the tourist season, and the hot and humid weather lead to increased travel and large gatherings, while many activities take place in enclosed spaces with air conditioning. These factors increase the risk of transmitting respiratory diseases, especially COVID-19 and seasonal influenza. Although most cases of COVID-19 and seasonal influenza are mild and resolve after treatment, the disease can still become severe in the elderly, young children, pregnant women, people with cardiovascular disease, chronic lung disease, diabetes, kidney disease, immunocompromised individuals, or those undergoing cancer treatment. To proactively protect their health, the Ministry of Health recommends that people wear masks when visiting medical facilities, on public transport, in crowded places or enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces; wash their hands frequently with soap or disinfectant, cover their mouths when coughing or sneezing, and avoid touching their eyes, nose, and mouth. In addition, people need to keep their living and working spaces well-ventilated, maintain a balanced diet, exercise regularly, get enough sleep, and manage underlying health conditions effectively. When experiencing symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, or fatigue, they should limit contact with others, proactively seek medical advice and examination when necessary, and avoid self-medication. You may also like The Department of Disease Prevention and Control stated that it will continue to coordinate with localities and medical facilities to closely monitor the situation of COVID-19, seasonal influenza, and variants of SARS-CoV-2 in order to promptly assess risks and implement appropriate disease prevention and control measures. The Ministry of Health advises people not to be complacent but also not to panic, and to proactively implement disease prevention measures to protect their own health, their families, and the community. news.content_title: Children remain more vulnerable to influenza despite protective antibody levels
news.content: Twice-weekly household testing across three influenza seasons shows why conventional antibody measures tell only part of the story about infection risk and prolonged viral shedding in children. Study: The roles of pre-season immunity, age, viral shedding, and community exposures in shaping influenza household transmission dynamics . Image Credit: Photoroyalty / Shutterstock In a recent study accepted for publication in the journal Nature Communications , researchers investigated the interplay between pre-season immunity, exposure intensity, viral shedding kinetics, and age in shaping the transmission dynamics of household influenza. The study’s analysis drew on the Prospective Household cohort study of Influenza, Respiratory Syncytial virus, and other respiratory pathogens community burden and Transmission dynamics in South Africa ( PHIRST ) cohort and comprised data from 1,518 participants across 327 households in rural and urban communities. The study’s findings revealed that pre-season serum hemagglutination inhibition ( HAI ) titers of at least 1:40 were associated with a reduced risk of infection for three of the four viruses studied. Furthermore, children exhibited age-dependent susceptibility and prolonged viral RNA shedding even after the models accounted for pre-season HAI antibody levels. Background Influenza has been recognized for decades as a major global respiratory health threat. However, because of the virus’s short shedding windows and high rates of asymptomatic infection, scientists have had difficulty characterizing key aspects of its real-world transmission dynamics. Previous research also indicates that traditional household transmission studies often overlook subclinical transmission events or rely on post-symptomatic clinical sampling. These limitations complicate efforts to develop comprehensive transmission models capable of disentangling how pre-existing humoral immunity, time-resolved viral shedding within households, and general community exposure are jointly associated with individual infection risk. About the Study The present study aimed to address these empirical uncertainties and inform future influenza prevention research by examining how measured immunity, age, viral shedding, and exposure were associated with the pathogen’s real-world transmission dynamics. The study dataset was obtained from PHIRST and included 1,518 participants across 327 households. PHIRST combined pre-season serum collection with twice-weekly virological testing of participants regardless of symptoms across three consecutive influenza seasons, 2016–2018. Viral shedding trajectories were subsequently modeled for 623 distinct infection episodes covering two influenza A subtypes and two influenza B lineages: A(H1N1)pdm09 (n = 133), A(H3N2) (n = 195), B/Victoria (n = 220), and B/Yamagata (n = 75). Multiplex real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction ( rRT-PCR ) cycle threshold ( Ct ) values were used in Bayesian hierarchical piecewise-linear models, thereby enabling estimation of the rise-to-peak viral shedding and the subsequent clearance phase for each infection episode. These shedding parameters were subsequently integrated into daily multivariable transmission survival models to simultaneously quantify: 1. Household force of infection ( FOI ; the sum of infected household members’ estimated daily shedding intensities), 2. Community FOI (daily, site-specific cohort infection prevalence), 3. Pre-season HAI titers (≥1:40 versus <1:40), and 4. Individual demographic factors (age, sex, household size, and HIV status). Study Findings The study’s multivariable transmission survival models showed that exposure intensity was strongly associated with infection acquisition. Specifically, each 10-unit increase in the modeled household shedding-intensity measure was associated with a 65% to 95% higher infection hazard across subtypes and lineages, for example, A(H1N1)pdm09 hazard ratio ( HR ) 1.96, 95% confidence interval ( CI ): 1.58–2.44; B/Victoria HR 1.77, 95% CI : 1.42–2.20. Similarly, a one-percentage-point increase in site-specific cohort influenza prevalence, used as a proxy for community exposure, was associated with a 70% to 100% increase in infection risk across all four subtypes and lineages. In addition, participants with a pre-season HAI titer ≥1:40 had a significantly lower infection risk for three out of the four investigated circulating viruses. This elevated HAI titer was associated with a 70% reduction in acquisition risk for A(H1N1)pdm09 ( HR 0.30), 35% for A(H3N2) ( HR 0.65), and 52% for B/Victoria ( HR 0.48). However, the categorical threshold of 1:40 was not significantly associated with a lower risk for B/Yamagata, although higher titers were associated with lower risk when analyzed as a continuous variable. Age remained strongly associated with infection risk even after adjustment for exposure levels and baseline titers. Notably, children younger than 5 years had an estimated 170% to 460% higher risk of infection with A(H1N1)pdm09, B/Victoria, and B/Yamagata compared with adults older than 40 years. Children younger than 5 years were also estimated to shed viral RNA for 3 to 5 days longer than older adults for A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria after adjustment for pre-season HAI titer status. Conclusions The present study showed that pre-season serum HAI titers were associated with reduced influenza acquisition for three of the four viruses studied, while age remained associated with infection risk after adjustment for measured household and community exposures and HAI titers, and with shedding duration after adjustment for HAI titers and other individual factors. The study’s authors noted that the dataset was limited by the absence of detailed intra-household contact network tracking. The study also had 2- to 3-day sampling gaps and used Ct values as indirect proxies for viral load , which may have led to very short infections being missed and introduced uncertainty into viral-load estimates. Additional limitations included assuming that HAI titers remained constant throughout each season, excluding coinfections, using infections detected within the cohort as a proxy for community exposure, and having fewer B/Yamagata infections. The statistical analyses were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. The absence of current-season vaccination among participants and the use of pre- COVID-19 data may also limit the applicability of the findings to other populations and periods. The authors therefore suggested that further research should examine age-appropriate correlates of protection and immune mechanisms beyond serum HAI antibodies, including antibodies targeting neuraminidase and the HA stalk, as well as influenza-specific B- and T-cell memory. Journal reference: Sauter, M. K., et al. (2026). The roles of pre-season immunity, age, viral shedding, and community exposures in shaping influenza household transmission dynamics. Nature Communications . DOI : 10.1038/s41467-026-76037-x. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-76037-x

analysis_zh.time: 该研究在 2016 年至 2018 年连续三个流感季节进行,每周测试两次。该研究结果已被《自然通讯》接受发表,但所提供的证据中没有报告确切的发表日期。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 该研究是在南非使用 PHIRST 队列研究 进行的,包括农村和城市社区 327 个家庭的 1,518 名参与者。该分析包括 623 起涉及儿童和成人的不同感染事件。
analysis_zh.event: 发表在《自然通讯》上的一项研究调查了季前免疫力、年龄、病毒脱落和社区暴露在塑造流感家庭 传播 动态中的作用。研究发现,尽管儿童具有保护性抗体水平,但仍然更容易感染流感,与成人相比,儿童的病毒脱落时间更长,感染风险更高。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 该研究分析了四种流感病毒的 623 次感染事件:甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09 (n=133)、甲型H3N2流感病毒 (n=195)、B/Victoria (n=220) 和 B/Yamagata (n=75)。与 40 岁以上的成年人相比,5 岁以下儿童感染 甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09、B/Victoria 和 B/Yamagata 的风险高出 170% 至 460%。对于这四种病毒中的三种病毒,儿童释放病毒 RNA 的时间比老年人长 3 至 5 天。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该研究使用多重实时 rRT-PCR 来模拟病毒脱落轨迹,并使用贝叶斯分层分段线性模型来估计感染风险。局限性包括缺乏详细的家庭内接触者追踪、2-3 天的采样间隔以及使用 Ct 值作为病毒载量的间接指标。由于缺乏当前季节的 疫苗接种 数据和 COVID-19 之前的研究期,可能会限制对其他人群的适用性。

Home News Breaking news Seven‐year‐old boy in critical condition with severe influenza A complications Breaking news Local Seven‐year‐old boy in critical condition with severe influenza A complications By Erwin Wong - 8:31PM Mon August 3, 2026 176 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Pinterest Telegram close Advertisements dimsumdailyhk [custom chain] curation-20260730-09:54 CANCEL NEXT VIDEO 3rd August 2026 – (Hong Kong) A seven‐year‐old boy is in critical condition after contracting a severe strain of influenza A, prompting health officials to remind the public to remain vigilant as seasonal flu activity intensifies. The Centre for Health Protection (CHP) announced today that it is investigating the serious paediatric case. The child, previously in good health, began experiencing a cough and runny nose on 27th July and developed a fever on 1st August. His condition worsened sharply on Monday, when he became less responsive and was taken to the Accident and Emergency Department at Princess Margaret Hospital. He was subsequently admitted to the paediatric intensive care unit. Laboratory tests confirmed infection with influenza A (H3). Doctors diagnosed influenza A complicated by shock and encephalopathy. The boy remains hospitalised in a critical state. Preliminary inquiries indicate that the child had received the 2025/26 seasonal influenza vaccination and had not travelled during the incubation period. One household member recently developed mild upper respiratory symptoms and tested positive for influenza using a rapid antigen test, but recovered without requiring hospital care. The CHP said investigations are ongoing. Hong Kong entered its influenza season in late June. According to the latest surveillance data, 10.65 per cent of respiratory specimens tested positive for seasonal influenza viruses last week, while the admission rate for influenza in public hospitals stood at 0.67 cases per 10,000 population. Both figures represent an increase compared with the previous week. Influenza A (H3) accounted for 48 per cent of detected cases, followed by influenza A (H1) at 41 per cent and influenza B at 11 per cent. Officials expect flu activity to remain elevated in the weeks ahead. Dr Edwin Tsui, Controller of the CHP, noted that the World Health Organisation has issued recommendations for the composition of the 2026‐2027 influenza vaccines for the northern hemisphere, with manufacturers now preparing supplies for deployment later this year. The Government is also making arrangements for the forthcoming 2026/27 Seasonal Influenza Vaccination Programme, with further details to be released in due course. Dr Tsui urged members of the public, particularly children, older people and individuals with underlying medical conditions or weakened immune systems, to seek prompt medical attention if they develop fever or respiratory symptoms, as deterioration can occur rapidly. Those living with vulnerable individuals should wear surgical masks at home if unwell and consult a doctor without delay. He also stressed the importance of maintaining household cleanliness, disinfecting frequently touched surfaces, practising proper hand hygiene and ensuring adequate indoor ventilation. news.content_title: Influenza A, Metapneumovirus, and Influenza B dominate respiratory virus circulation in Delhi NCR
news.content: Medical experts in Delhi NCR have reported a widespread circulation of respiratory viruses, with Influenza A (H3N2) identified as the primary cause of the current surge. This wave features severe symptoms, including high-grade fevers and recovery periods often extending beyond 10 days. Dr Arjun Dang, CEO of Dr Dang’s Lab, named Influenza A (H3N2), Metapneumovirus, Coronaviruses, and Influenza B as the main viral agents present in the region. He associated the surge with cooler temperatures, fluctuating humidity, and increasing air pollution, conditions that encourage gatherings in crowded indoor spaces. - BJP chief Nitin Nabin pledges introspection after Bankipur and Datia by-polls, welcomes Gujarat win - Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar assures excluded Congress leaders will receive appropriate roles - Parliamentary panel chief urges Zuckerberg to apologise for removal of PM Modi’s video or face loss of safe harbour protection Dr Dhiren Gupta, a paediatric specialist at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, noted that more than 50% of children in outpatient departments present symptoms such as fever, cough, and body aches. Speaking to ANI, Dr Arjun Dang said, “The respiratory pathogen pattern shows predominant circulation of viral agents, particularly Influenza A (H3N2), Metapneumovirus, Coronaviruses, and Influenza B, which aligns with the changing weather in Delhi NCR marked by cooler temperatures, fluctuating humidity and rising air pollution leading to increased indoor crowding. The concurrent detection of multiple respiratory viruses suggests seasonal co-circulation/co-infections rather than isolated outbreaks, a pattern commonly observed during post-monsoon and winter transitions, while sporadic detection of Mycoplasma pneumoniae likely reflects background transmission or a secondary bacterial infection facilitated due to the immunocompromised state during viral infections.” Dr Dhiren Gupta, Paediatric Intensive Care Specialist, Pulmonologist and Allergist, said, “There has been a noticeable rise in influenza cases, including H3N2 virus infection, in India over the past month. In our outpatient department, more than 50% of children are currently presenting with symptoms of influenza such as fever, cough, cold, sore throat, and body ache.” He added, “The good news is that most of these cases are mild and self-limiting. At present, there is no significant increase in hospitalisation, and the majority of children are recovering well with routine care.” He advised parents to monitor their children and seek medical advice promptly if fever persists. “Parents are advised not to panic. Adequate hydration, good nutrition, and proper rest are important for recovery. Early consultation with a doctor is recommended if a child has a high fever, breathing difficulty, poor oral intake, or symptoms lasting more than a few days,” he said. Dr Dhiren also stressed the importance of hygiene and preventive measures to limit virus transmission: “Simple preventive measures such as regular hand washing, wearing masks in crowded places, and avoiding close contact with sick individuals can help reduce the spread of infection.”

supplementary_news.content: Twice-weekly household testing across three influenza seasons shows why conventional antibody measures tell only part of the story about infection risk and prolonged viral shedding in children. Study: The roles of pre-season immunity, age, viral shedding, and community exposures in shaping influenza household transmission dynamics . Image Credit: Photoroyalty / Shutterstock In a recent study accepted for publication in the journal Nature Communications , researchers investigated the interplay between pre-season immunity, exposure intensity, viral shedding kinetics, and age in shaping the transmission dynamics of household influenza. The study’s analysis drew on the Prospective Household cohort study of Influenza, Respiratory Syncytial virus, and other respiratory pathogens community burden and Transmission dynamics in South Africa ( PHIRST ) cohort and comprised data from 1,518 participants across 327 households in rural and urban communities. The study’s findings revealed that pre-season serum hemagglutination inhibition ( HAI ) titers of at least 1:40 were associated with a reduced risk of infection for three of the four viruses studied. Furthermore, children exhibited age-dependent susceptibility and prolonged viral RNA shedding even after the models accounted for pre-season HAI antibody levels. Background Influenza has been recognized for decades as a major global respiratory health threat. However, because of the virus’s short shedding windows and high rates of asymptomatic infection, scientists have had difficulty characterizing key aspects of its real-world transmission dynamics. Previous research also indicates that traditional household transmission studies often overlook subclinical transmission events or rely on post-symptomatic clinical sampling. These limitations complicate efforts to develop comprehensive transmission models capable of disentangling how pre-existing humoral immunity, time-resolved viral shedding within households, and general community exposure are jointly associated with individual infection risk. About the Study The present study aimed to address these empirical uncertainties and inform future influenza prevention research by examining how measured immunity, age, viral shedding, and exposure were associated with the pathogen’s real-world transmission dynamics. The study dataset was obtained from PHIRST and included 1,518 participants across 327 households. PHIRST combined pre-season serum collection with twice-weekly virological testing of participants regardless of symptoms across three consecutive influenza seasons, 2016–2018. Viral shedding trajectories were subsequently modeled for 623 distinct infection episodes covering two influenza A subtypes and two influenza B lineages: A(H1N1)pdm09 (n = 133), A(H3N2) (n = 195), B/Victoria (n = 220), and B/Yamagata (n = 75). Multiplex real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction ( rRT-PCR ) cycle threshold ( Ct ) values were used in Bayesian hierarchical piecewise-linear models, thereby enabling estimation of the rise-to-peak viral shedding and the subsequent clearance phase for each infection episode. These shedding parameters were subsequently integrated into daily multivariable transmission survival models to simultaneously quantify: 1. Household force of infection ( FOI ; the sum of infected household members’ estimated daily shedding intensities), 2. Community FOI (daily, site-specific cohort infection prevalence), 3. Pre-season HAI titers (≥1:40 versus <1:40), and 4. Individual demographic factors (age, sex, household size, and HIV status). Study Findings The study’s multivariable transmission survival models showed that exposure intensity was strongly associated with infection acquisition. Specifically, each 10-unit increase in the modeled household shedding-intensity measure was associated with a 65% to 95% higher infection hazard across subtypes and lineages, for example, A(H1N1)pdm09 hazard ratio ( HR ) 1.96, 95% confidence interval ( CI ): 1.58–2.44; B/Victoria HR 1.77, 95% CI : 1.42–2.20. Similarly, a one-percentage-point increase in site-specific cohort influenza prevalence, used as a proxy for community exposure, was associated with a 70% to 100% increase in infection risk across all four subtypes and lineages. In addition, participants with a pre-season HAI titer ≥1:40 had a significantly lower infection risk for three out of the four investigated circulating viruses. This elevated HAI titer was associated with a 70% reduction in acquisition risk for A(H1N1)pdm09 ( HR 0.30), 35% for A(H3N2) ( HR 0.65), and 52% for B/Victoria ( HR 0.48). However, the categorical threshold of 1:40 was not significantly associated with a lower risk for B/Yamagata, although higher titers were associated with lower risk when analyzed as a continuous variable. Age remained strongly associated with infection risk even after adjustment for exposure levels and baseline titers. Notably, children younger than 5 years had an estimated 170% to 460% higher risk of infection with A(H1N1)pdm09, B/Victoria, and B/Yamagata compared with adults older than 40 years. Children younger than 5 years were also estimated to shed viral RNA for 3 to 5 days longer than older adults for A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria after adjustment for pre-season HAI titer status. Conclusions The present study showed that pre-season serum HAI titers were associated with reduced influenza acquisition for three of the four viruses studied, while age remained associated with infection risk after adjustment for measured household and community exposures and HAI titers, and with shedding duration after adjustment for HAI titers and other individual factors. The study’s authors noted that the dataset was limited by the absence of detailed intra-household contact network tracking. The study also had 2- to 3-day sampling gaps and used Ct values as indirect proxies for viral load , which may have led to very short infections being missed and introduced uncertainty into viral-load estimates. Additional limitations included assuming that HAI titers remained constant throughout each season, excluding coinfections, using infections detected within the cohort as a proxy for community exposure, and having fewer B/Yamagata infections. The statistical analyses were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. The absence of current-season vaccination among participants and the use of pre- COVID-19 data may also limit the applicability of the findings to other populations and periods. The authors therefore suggested that further research should examine age-appropriate correlates of protection and immune mechanisms beyond serum HAI antibodies, including antibodies targeting neuraminidase and the HA stalk, as well as influenza-specific B- and T-cell memory. Journal reference: Sauter, M. K., et al. (2026). The roles of pre-season immunity, age, viral shedding, and community exposures in shaping influenza household transmission dynamics. Nature Communications . DOI : 10.1038/s41467-026-76037-x. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-76037-x
